summary: Defines an experimental portion of the MIB for managing OSI connectionless networks (ISO 8473 and ISO 9542). It is an Experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1238 adds a set of standard values that a network manager can read over SNMP from a router running the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol. It covers counters for traffic, tables of addresses and routes, and counters for the routing exchange between end systems and routers.

questions: how does snmp read managed objects
what changed between rfc 1162 and rfc 1238
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching an OSI connectionless network and its routing exchanges.

tldr.problem: Managers of networks that use the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol had no standard set of values they could read over SNMP to see what those networks were doing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines managed objects under a new branch of the Management Information Base: counters for the protocol data units sent and received, tables of addresses and routes, and counters for the error protocol and for the ES-IS routing exchange.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that obsoletes RFC 1162, and it says so itself: discussion and suggestions for improvement are requested.

facts.label: Default NSAP
facts.value: A single octet with the value 0

today: RFC 1238 is an Experimental document. It obsoletes RFC 1162 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It adds objects to the standard Management Information Base rather than defining a new protocol, so what it describes is what a management station can read from a system running the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol and the ES-IS routing exchange.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 1238 defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. The status of the memo is an Experimental Protocol for the Internet community, and it asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement. It obsoletes RFC 1162 and its title names the two protocols it covers: the Connectionless Network Protocol, ISO 8473, and the End System to Intermediate System routing exchange, ISO 9542.

The memo starts by setting out the framework the new objects sit in, which has three parts. RFC 1155 defines the Structure of Management Information (SMI), the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management. RFC 1212 defines a more concise description mechanism that is wholly consistent with the SMI. RFC 1156 defines MIB-I, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, and RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, an evolution of MIB-I based on implementation experience and new operational requirements. RFC 1157 defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects.

The framework explicitly permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation, which is the licence this memo uses. The objects defined here are meant to be used when the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol and the End System to Intermediate System protocol are present. The memo makes no assumption about which underlying protocol carries the SNMP traffic itself.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP already has a standard way of naming and describing the values a device exposes. This memo adds new values to that scheme, so that a manager can watch an ISO connectionless network with the same tools used for everything else.

sections.title: How Managed Objects Are Described
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. The memo explains the three things every object type has. Its name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name that specifies an object type; the object type together with an object instance then identifies one specific instantiation of it. For human convenience a textual string, called the OBJECT DESCRIPTOR, can be used to refer to the object type as well.

The syntax of an object type defines the abstract data structure behind it. The ASN.1 language is used for that purpose, but the SMI restricts which ASN.1 constructs may be used, and the memo says those restrictions are made explicitly for simplicity. The encoding of an object type is how that type is represented using its syntax, and how it is represented when transmitted on the network. The SMI specifies the use of the basic encoding rules of ASN.1, subject to further requirements imposed by SNMP.

Section 4 of the memo then specifies every object type in the module using the conventions of the SMI, as amended by the extensions in RFC 1212.
sections.plainLanguage: Every value a device exposes has three parts: a name that identifies it, a syntax that says what kind of value it is, and an encoding that says how it is written on the wire. SNMP adds its own requirements on top of the ASN.1 rules that ASN.1 already defines.

sections.title: The ClnpAddress Type
sections.content:
The memo introduces one new data type, as a textual convention that makes the specification easier to read and easier to compare with other specifications. The memo is careful about what this does and does not change: the introduction of the textual convention has no effect on the syntax or the semantics of any managed object, and objects defined in these terms are still encoded by the rules of the underlying primitive type. No change to the SMI or to SNMP is needed to accommodate it.

The type ClnpAddress is used to denote an OSI address, and it consists of a string of octets. The first octet holds a binary value in the range 0 to 20 and says how many octets the NSAP occupies. The NSAP follows, expressed in concrete binary notation starting with the most significant octet. A zero-length NSAP is used as a special address meaning the default NSAP, which the memo compares to the IP address 0.0.0.0; it is encoded as a single octet containing the value 0. All other NSAPs are encoded in at least four octets. The type is declared as ClnpAddress ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (1..21)).
sections.plainLanguage: An OSI address is written as a string of bytes. The first byte says how long the address is, and a zero-length address stands for the default one, the way 0.0.0.0 stands for the default IP address.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 1162
sections.content:
The memo lists four differences from RFC 1162, the document it replaces.

First, the managed objects are defined using the conventions of the Internet-standard SMI as amended by the extensions specified in RFC 1212. The memo emphasises that definitions made using those extensions are semantically identical to those in RFC 1162, so the change is one of notation rather than of meaning.

Second, the PhysAddress textual convention from MIB-II has been introduced to represent media addresses.

Third, three objects that RFC 1162 did not have have been defined: clnpRoutingDiscards, clnpRouteMetric5 and clnpRouteInfo.

Fourth, a mistake was fixed. The ClnpAddress type was mistakenly given a tag in RFC 1162, and that error has been corrected here.
sections.plainLanguage: The new version of this MIB is almost identical to the one it replaces. It is written in a tidier notation, it adds three objects, and it repairs a mistake in how one type was tagged.

sections.title: The Groups of Managed Objects
sections.content:
The definitions sit under a single new branch of the object identifier tree, clns OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { experimental 1 }, which divides into four groups: clnp at { clns 1 }, error at { clns 2 }, echo at { clns 3 } and es-is at { clns 4 }. The echo branch is reserved in the tree but no objects are defined under it in this memo.

The CLNP group is the largest, and the memo recommends implementing it on all systems that implement CLNP. It starts with two writable settings: clnpForwarding, an integer that says whether the entity is an intermediate system that forwards protocol data units onward, or an end system that does not, and clnpDefaultLifeTime, the default value inserted into the Lifetime field of the CLNP header of packets the entity sends.

Then come the counters. On the way in: protocol data units received from all connected interfaces, those discarded because of header errors such as bad checksums or lifetime exceeded, those discarded because the destination address was not valid here, those forwarded onward, those discarded because the network or upper layer protocol was unknown, those discarded for other reasons, and those delivered. On the way out: requests, discards, and packets with no route. Further counters cover reassembly timeouts and successes and failures, segmentation successes, failures and created segments, options present, and routing discards.

Four tables follow. The address table maps the addresses the entity uses to their interface index and the reassembly size in use. The routing table has a row per route, with the destination, the interface, four metrics, the next hop, the type of route, the protocol that learned it, the age of the entry, a fifth metric and a reference to MIB definitions specific to that routing protocol. The route type is one of other, invalid, direct for a connected network, or remote for a non-local host, network or sub-network. The route protocol names where the route came from, among them local for manually configured entries, netmgmt, is-is, ciscoIgrp, bbnSpfIgp, ospf and bgp, and the memo notes that listing gateway routing protocols does not imply that hosts should support them. Setting the type to invalid dissolves the destination from the route, and a management station must be prepared to receive table entries that are not in use.

The two address translation tables hold the equivalences between CLNP addresses and physical addresses, one mapping each way. The memo notes that some interfaces do not use translation tables at all, in which case the table is simply empty.

The CLNP Error group counts error protocol data units sent and received, split by cause: unspecified, protocol errors, checksum errors, congestion, header errors, segmentation errors, incompatible packets, duplicates, unreachable and unknown destinations, errors in source and record route fields, hop counts and hop reassembly, unsupported options, unsupported versions, unsupported security options, and reassembly interference. The ES-IS group is six counters: ESH, ISH and RDU protocol data units sent and received. The memo recommends implementing it on all systems that implement the End System to Intermediate System protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The new objects are arranged in four groups. One holds counters for the packets the router sends and receives, plus tables of its addresses and its routes. Another counts error messages by cause. The third counts the routing exchange between end systems and routers. The fourth is reserved for later use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The memo defines what a manager can read and, in a few places, what it can write, such as the forwarding mode, the default lifetime and the routing table, but it says nothing about who is allowed to read those values or to change them. That question is left to the management protocol itself and to whatever protections the site has around it.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. It describes which values a manager can read and change, but says nothing about who should be allowed to do so.
